Explanation: The ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum) gives rise to the collecting ducts, the minor and major calyces, the renal pelvis, and the ureter; nephron segments arise separately from the metanephric mesenchyme.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Metanephric diverticulum derivatives
Notes: Confirmed: Kispert, Nat Rev Nephrol 2025; Little et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2016. Board overlap: pair carefully with NEPH-002 on the same 16-tile board.

Explanation: The metanephric mesenchyme (blastema) forms the nephron from the glomerulus through the distal convoluted tubule; the collecting duct derives from the ureteric bud.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Metanephric blastema derivatives; Nephron progenitor derivatives
Notes: Confirmed: Little et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2016; Kispert, Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Board overlap with NEPH-001 (ureteric bud derivatives).

Explanation: All inhibit the luminal Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: NKCC2 inhibitors; Thick ascending limb diuretics
Notes: Confirmed: Agarwal et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Competing category: shared ototoxicity (ambiguity 1). Ethacrynic acid is the non-sulfonamide loop agent; do not label the set as sulfonamides. Avoid pairing with an ototoxicity category on one board.

Explanation: These drugs inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) in the early distal convoluted tubule and reduce urinary calcium excretion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: NCC inhibitors; Early DCT diuretics
Notes: Confirmed: Agarwal et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Chlorthalidone and metolazone are thiazide-like; title includes them. Competing category: calcium-retaining diuretics (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: All reduce distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, through mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade (spironolactone, eplerenone) or ENaC inhibition (amiloride, triamterene).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Distal potassium-retaining diuretics; ENaC/MR-targeting distal diuretics
Notes: Confirmed: Agarwal et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Two mechanisms within the set; unifying relationship is the shared potassium-sparing effect. Competing category: drugs causing hyperkalemic (type 4-like) metabolic acidosis. Heart-failure mortality benefit applies only to the MRAs.

Explanation: Defective proximal tubular transport (rBAT/b0,+AT) increases urinary loss of the COLA group; poor cystine solubility is responsible for stone formation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: COLA transport defect; Cystinuria transport substrates
Notes: Confirmed: Dahl & Goldfarb, Evidence-Based Nephrology 2022; Bargagli et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Only cystine is poorly soluble and forms stones; title correctly frames the shared transport defect rather than chemistry (cystine is not a dibasic amino acid).

Explanation: Marked glomerular protein loss lowers serum albumin and promotes edema; altered lipid metabolism produces hyperlipidemia. Adult nephrotic-range proteinuria is typically above 3.5 g/day.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Classic nephrotic syndrome tetrad
Source Section: Nephrotic Syndromes > Glomerular Disease Overview (PDF pp. 57)
Notes: Confirmed: KDIGO 2021; Vivarelli et al., CJASN 2017. Lipiduria is a 5th classic feature not required here.

Connection Title: Minimal change disease biopsy and urine clues
Explanation: Minimal change disease combines bland light microscopy and negative immune-deposit staining with diffuse foot-process effacement and relatively selective albumin loss.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: MCD diagnostic pattern
Source Section: Nephrotic Syndromes > Minimal Change Disease (PDF pp. 52, 58)
Notes: Confirmed: Vivarelli et al., CJASN 2017; KDIGO 2021. Albumin selectivity is typical, especially in children (less selective in adults). Foot-process effacement is nonspecific (also FSGS); the combined pattern carries the specificity (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Each is an established cause of secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or an FSGS-pattern lesion; mechanism and frequency differ among them.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Secondary FSGS associations; Secondary FSGS causes
Source Section: Nephrotic Syndromes > Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (PDF pp. 52, 56, 59)
Notes: Lowered from candidate ambiguity 2 to 1 on independent review. All four confirmed: Kim et al., Biomed Res Int 2015; D Agati et al., NEJM 2011; KDIGO 2021. Qualifiers: HIV and interferon classically cause the collapsing variant; heroin-associated FSGS is historical with adulterant confounding; sickle cell FSGS is hyperfiltration-mediated. Board overlap: do not combine with a collapsing-glomerulopathy category (HIV and interferon would double-fit).

Explanation: These are recognized associations of secondary membranous nephropathy spanning infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy, and drug exposure; lupus-associated membranous disease corresponds to ISN/RPS class V.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Secondary membranous nephropathy associations; Secondary membranous nephropathy causes
Notes: Confirmed: KDIGO 2021; Moroni & Ponticelli, Front Med 2020; FDA penicillamine label (Cuprimine/Depen). PLA2R is typically negative in secondary disease. Board overlap: HBV and SLE also cause other glomerular lesions.

Explanation: Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits, capillary-wall thickening, and granular staining; anti-PLA2R supports PLA2R-associated disease and is not present in every case.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PLA2R-associated membranous nephropathy clues; Membranous nephropathy diagnostic pattern
Notes: Confirmed: Ronco et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021; KDIGO 2021. Anti-PLA2R is subtype-dependent (positive in ~70% of primary disease), not universal. Granular IgG/C3 overlaps with other immune-complex GN (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: PSGN follows a nephritogenic streptococcal infection and classically produces complement consumption with subepithelial deposits and granular staining.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PSGN diagnostic associations; Acute postinfectious GN clues
Notes: Low C3 and biopsy features are typical, not obligatory; C3 normalizes by ~8 weeks. Overlaps with other infection-related GN (staphylococcal, endocarditis-associated). Latency ~1-3 wk post-pharyngitis vs ~3-6 wk post-impetigo (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: A type IV collagen disorder (COL4A3/4/5) can affect glomerular, cochlear, and ocular structures; electron microscopy may show basket-weave splitting of the glomerular basement membrane.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Type IV collagen nephropathy findings; Alport syndrome clues
Notes: Extrarenal findings are genotype/age/sex-dependent (most consistent in X-linked males) and are not present in every patient. Anterior lenticonus is highly specific. No competing syndrome of equal strength.

Explanation: Cystinuria causes cystine stone formation, characteristically hexagonal urinary crystals, and a positive nitroprusside screen; stones are faintly radiopaque owing to sulfur content.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cystine stone clues; Cystinuria stone findings
Notes: Confirmed: Dahl & Goldfarb, Evidence-Based Nephrology 2022; Bargagli et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025; Howles & Thakker, Nat Rev Urol 2020. Cystine stones are faintly radiopaque (reduced opacity vs calcium stones), not radiolucent. Nitroprusside screen is sensitive but not fully specific.

Explanation: Urease generates ammonia and raises urinary pH, promoting magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitation; the resulting stones may fill the collecting system.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Infection stone clues; Magnesium ammonium phosphate stone clues
Notes: Confirmed: Bargagli et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025; Coe et al., NEJM 1992. Not all struvite stones are staghorn and not all staghorn stones are struvite (cystine and uric acid can also form staghorns). Alkaline urine is nonspecific (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Oxalate production or absorption can rise with ethylene glycol, high vitamin C intake, and fat malabsorption (enteric hyperoxaluria); low urinary citrate removes an inhibitor of calcium crystallization.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Calcium oxalate stone promoters; Calcium oxalate risk exposures
Notes: Confirmed: Bargagli et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Qualifier retained: ethylene glycol often causes acute oxalate nephropathy/crystalluria rather than typical colic. Hypocitraturia also promotes calcium phosphate stones (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Each can compromise the vulnerable renal papilla through ischemic, infectious, or analgesic-related injury and predispose to papillary necrosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Papillary necrosis risk factors; Papillary ischemia risk factors
Source Section: Kidney Injury > Renal Papillary Necrosis (PDF pp. 86, 95, 100)
Notes: Confirmed core POSTCARDS members: Griffin et al., JASN 1995; Eknoyan et al., Medicine 1982. Qualifier retained: NSAID/analgesic association requires chronic high-dose exposure. Each member causes other renal lesions as well (ambiguity 1).

Connection Title: Medications that can cause acute interstitial nephritis
Explanation: These agents or classes are associated with drug-induced tubulointerstitial inflammation and acute kidney injury.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Drug-induced AIN triggers
Source Section: Kidney Injury > Acute Interstitial Nephritis (PDF pp. 54, 86, 89, 92, 116)
Notes: Confirmed drug-induced AIN agents. NSAID-associated AIN often lacks the classic hypersensitivity triad and may carry concurrent minimal-change-type nephrotic proteinuria. Risk varies by agent and exposure (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: These can directly injure renal tubular cells causing acute tubular injury; myoglobin-mediated tubular injury occurs in rhabdomyolysis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nephrotoxic acute tubular injury causes; Direct tubular toxins
Source Section: Kidney Injury > Acute Tubular Necrosis (PDF pp. 54, 86, 89, 93)
Notes: Confirmed direct tubular toxins. Amphotericin B also causes afferent vasoconstriction and distal electrolyte wasting; myoglobin is an endogenous pigment (rhabdomyolysis). Title intentionally says exposures (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Preserved tubular sodium and water retention during reduced renal perfusion often yields concentrated urine, low sodium excretion, and a disproportionate BUN elevation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Prerenal azotemia laboratory pattern; Sodium-avid AKI pattern
Notes: Represents the typical untreated pattern; no single threshold is diagnostic. Diuretics, CKD, sepsis, diet, bleeding, and timing alter results. FENa below 1% also occurs in contrast/pigment nephropathy and early AIN/GN (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Accumulated uremic toxins in advanced kidney failure can cause pericarditis, central nervous system dysfunction (encephalopathy), peripheral neuropathy, and platelet dysfunction with a bleeding tendency.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Symptomatic uremia manifestations; Uremic syndrome complications
Source Section: Kidney Injury > Chronic Kidney Disease (PDF pp. 54, 87, 96)
Notes: REVISED: replaced Asterixis with Peripheral neuropathy. Asterixis is a sign of uremic encephalopathy (Wijdicks, J Intern Med 2022), so it overlapped the Encephalopathy tile and failed the distinct-tile rule. Uremic peripheral neuropathy, pericarditis, encephalopathy, and platelet dysfunction are all established uremic complications (Vanholder et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2016; Rehman et al., Clin Cardiol 2017). Uremic pericarditis and bleeding are classic dialysis indications.

Explanation: ADPKD is associated with extrarenal cysts and selected vascular, valvular, and gastrointestinal abnormalities; these findings are not universal.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Extrarenal ADPKD manifestations; Extrarenal polycystic kidney disease findings
Source Section: Cystic Kidney Disease > Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease
Notes: Confirmed: Chebib et al., JAMA 2025; Harris & Torres, GeneReviews. Hepatic cysts most common (~94% over age 35); intracranial aneurysms ~9-12%; MVP reported up to ~25% (lower with modern criteria); diverticulosis strongest in ESRD. Strength varies (ambiguity 1). Input note: original Source Section lacked PDF page numbers.

Explanation: RCC can be associated with production of mediators causing hypercalcemia (PTHrP), erythrocytosis (EPO), hypercortisolism (ACTH), or hypertension (renin).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: RCC paraneoplastic mediators; RCC PEAR mediators
Source Section: Inflammatory Conditions & Malignancy > Renal Cell Carcinoma (PDF pp. 98, 102)
Notes: Confirmed: Hegemann et al., World J Urol 2018; Rose & Kim, JAMA 2024. PTHrP and EPO common; ectopic ACTH (Cushing) and renin (hypertension) are rare/anecdotal (qualifier retained). Board overlap: hypercalcemia and erythrocytosis categories.

Explanation: These exposures are established urothelial cancer risks; cyclophosphamide toxicity involves urinary metabolites and phenacetin is a historical analgesic exposure.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Urothelial carcinoma risk exposures; Bladder and upper-tract urothelial carcinogens
Source Section: Inflammatory Conditions & Malignancy > Urothelial Carcinoma (PDF pp. 98, 105)
Notes: Confirmed: Lenis et al., JAMA 2020; van Hoogstraten et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol 2023. Phenacetin is a banned historical analgesic (aristolochic acid is a modern analogue, not listed). Risk is cumulative-dose dependent (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reduces aqueous humor and CSF production and increases renal bicarbonate loss, supporting these clinical uses.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor indications
Source Section: Renal Pharmacology > Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (PDF pp. 114)
Notes: Confirmed: Agarwal et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025. Role is adjunctive/variable by setting, not sole or first-line in each. Glaucoma and raised ICP overlap with osmotic-diuretic (mannitol) uses (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Each raises intra-abdominal pressure and can provoke leakage when urethral support or sphincter function is impaired.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pressure-provoked urinary leakage; Valsalva incontinence triggers
Notes: These are triggers in susceptible patients, not universal causes. Relatively low category specificity/depth (kept Easy). Board overlap: any Valsalva-maneuver category (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: GI bicarbonate loss and renal bicarbonate loss or impaired acid excretion can produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis without an increased anion gap.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis causes; Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis causes
Source Section: Acid-Base Physiology > Metabolic Acidosis; RTA Type 1; RTA Type 2 (PDF pp. 22, 40, 41, 42, 46, 47, 48, 49, 93, 118)
Notes: Confirmed: Berend et al., NEJM 2014; Palmer et al., Adv Ther 2021. Acetazolamide acts through a proximal-RTA-like mechanism, mechanistically overlapping the type 2 RTA tile, but the entities remain distinct. Board overlap: avoid combining with another RTA/NAGMA category (e.g., type 4) on one board (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Severe neuromuscular weakness (anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, or neuromuscular junction) can reduce alveolar ventilation, causing CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Neuromuscular respiratory failure; Respiratory weakness causing respiratory acidosis
Notes: REVISED: replaced Multiple sclerosis with Botulism, and refined the title. MS is a CNS demyelinating disease absent from neuromuscular respiratory-failure classifications; its respiratory failure is a late central-mechanism event (Tzelepis & McCool, Respir Med 2015). MG, ALS, GBS, and botulism are the classic neuromuscular causes (Wijdicks, Ann Neurol 2017; Mehta, Respir Care 2006). Competing category NMJ disorders fits only MG and botulism (ambiguity 1). Note: this physiology connection remains under the Renal/Urinary nephrology source bank but is cross-disciplinary with neurology/critical care.

Explanation: Reduced renal phosphate clearance, reduced PTH-mediated phosphaturia, or large intracellular phosphate release can increase serum phosphate.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hyperphosphatemia causes
Notes: Confirmed mechanisms of hyperphosphatemia. Competing category: all four can also associate with hypocalcemia, an equally plausible grouping; avoid pairing with a hypocalcemia category on one board. Levels depend on renal function, timing, and treatment (ambiguity 1).

Explanation: Diabetic kidney injury can produce nodular mesangial sclerosis, expanded mesangial matrix, thickened basement membrane, and podocyte injury; findings evolve with disease stage.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Diabetic nephropathy biopsy findings; Diabetic glomerulopathy pathology
Notes: Confirmed: Tervaert et al., JASN 2010 (Renal Pathology Society classification). Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (class III) are a specific form of mesangial expansion, so there is partial conceptual overlap with the mesangial-expansion tile; findings are stage-dependent and need not coexist early. Foot-process effacement is nonspecific (ambiguity 1).
